passage: At the end of the day at playschool, the van was honking outside. Kalyani sat on the low bench with one sandal on the wrong foot. Ritu Miss knelt to help. "No! Me do it!" Kalyani pulled her foot away. She tugged the strap, it slipped, she tugged again. Her tongue poked out. Ritu Miss sat back on her heels, waited, and called to the driver, "Two more minutes!" At last the strap clicked. Kalyani stood up, stamped both feet, and marched to the van, chin high.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say when Ritu Miss knelt to help?
qa.a: "No! Me do it!"

qa.q: What does Kalyani's stamping and chin held high suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and strong because she had done the strap by herself 😊.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu Miss make, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: She sat back, waited and asked the driver for two more minutes, letting Kalyani finish on her own.

qa.q: How might the van driver feel about the two extra minutes?
qa.a: The driver may be a bit impatient, but a short wait lets a small child leave feeling capable instead of upset.

grounding: A small girl at playschool insists on doing her own sandal strap while the van waits.

passage: I'm Mahima, Deepak's big sister. Every morning before school Papa says, "Quick, quick, we're late!" and every morning Deepak sits on the doorstep with his shoes and says, "I do it." He puts the left shoe on the right foot. He tries again. The laces are like noodles in his hands. Papa taps his watch. Today Papa reached down, and Deepak cried, "Mine!" and hugged his shoe. So Papa waited. When the last lace was a floppy bow, Deepak held up his foot like a trophy. We were late. He didn't care one bit.

qa.q: What did Deepak do when Papa reached down to help?
qa.a: Deepak cried, "Mine!" and hugged his shoe.

qa.q: Why did Deepak hold up his foot like a trophy?
qa.a: He felt proud that he'd done it himself, and that mattered more to him than being on time.

qa.q: What could Papa try on school mornings so Deepak can still do it himself?
qa.a: Papa could start shoe time a few minutes earlier, so Deepak can keep his 'I do it' without everyone rushing.

qa.q: How does Mahima see these mornings?
qa.a: Mahima watches with some amusement, noticing Papa's watch-tapping and Deepak not caring one bit about being late.

grounding: A big sister describes her small brother insisting on putting on his own shoes even when the family is late.

passage:
Monday: Vasudha's mother, Parul, was late for the bus and pushed Vasudha's feet into her shoes. Vasudha kicked and cried all the way to the stop. "I wanted to do it!"
Wednesday: Parul put the shoes out early by the door and said nothing. Vasudha sat and worked on them for a long time, grunting, the velcro sticking crooked. They were five minutes late. Vasudha was smiling.
Friday: Vasudha put her shoes on by herself, still crooked, and ran to show her mother. "Look! I did it all!" Parul laughed and fixed nothing.

qa.q: Where did Parul put the shoes on Wednesday?
qa.a: She put the shoes out early by the door.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha kick and cry on Monday?
qa.a: Vasudha felt angry and frustrated because she wanted to do it herself, and having her feet pushed into the shoes took that away.

qa.q: What change did Parul make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She set the shoes out early and stayed quiet, giving Vasudha time and space to do it by herself.

qa.q: How might Parul's week feel compared with Vasudha's?
qa.a: Parul feels the pressure of being late, but on Friday she sees her daughter proud and happy, which makes the waiting worth it.

grounding: Across a week, a small girl insists on doing her own shoes, and her mother makes room for it.

passage:
Rain drummed on the tin shade, and the school van was already honking at the gate. Yusuf held out Reena's shoes. 'Quick, Abbu will do it.'
'NO. Me do it.' Reena sat on the step and pushed the left shoe onto the right foot. Took it off. Tried again. Her tongue poked out.
Yusuf looked at the clock and breathed out. He crouched and held the shoe still, just still, while Reena pushed her foot in.
She stood up, stamped both feet and beamed. 'I did it!'
They ran through the puddles to the van, two minutes late.

qa.q: What was the weather while Reena put on her shoes?
qa.a: Rain was drumming on the tin shade.

qa.q: Why did Reena shout 'Me do it'?
qa.a: She badly wanted to do it herself; managing her own shoes made her feel big and capable, even with the van honking.

qa.q: What choice did Yusuf make that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of taking over, he held the shoe still while Reena pushed her foot in; she still did it herself, and they were only two minutes late.

qa.q: What would change for Reena if Yusuf had just put the shoes on for her?
qa.a: They might have caught the van on time, but Reena would likely have protested and missed that proud 'I did it!' moment.

grounding: A young child insists on putting on her own shoes while the van honks, and her father steadies the shoe instead of taking over.

passage:
In the lift lobby of their Pune building, the whole family was ready for Nani's birthday lunch, except for Parveen's shoes. The cab driver had called twice.
'Let me,' said Ujjwal bhaiya, bending down.
'I can DO it!' Parveen pulled the foot away and started on the buckle, missing the hole again and again.
Mumma opened her mouth, then shut it. 'Okay. Buckle's yours. Bhaiya holds the lift.'
Ujjwal held the lift door. Pin, hole, miss. Pin, hole... click.
Parveen looked up, face shining. 'Done! By myself!'
In the cab, Parveen kept swinging both feet to admire the buckles.

qa.q: Who held the lift door?
qa.a: Ujjwal bhaiya.

qa.q: Why did Parveen pull the foot away from Ujjwal bhaiya?
qa.a: Parveen wanted to do the buckle alone; doing it 'by myself' mattered more than being quick.

qa.q: What choice did Mumma make, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: Mumma gave Parveen the buckle and gave Ujjwal bhaiya the lift, so Parveen could finish while the family kept moving.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal bhaiya feel being pushed away when trying to help?
qa.a: He may feel a little brushed off, with the cab waiting, but holding the lift gave him a useful job as well.

grounding: A young child insists on doing a shoe buckle alone while the family is late, and a parent makes room for it.

passage: The school van was honking at the gate in Rajgarh, and Bhupen sat on the doorstep with one shoe on the wrong foot. 'Let me,' said his sister Swati, bending down. 'No! Myself!' passage: On a rainy Dublin morning, the bus to nursery was due in four minutes. Liam sat on the hall floor, wrestling with his green wellies. 'I'll do it, buddy,' said his dad, Rafael, reaching over. 'No. I do it.' Liam pushed his hand away and yanked the boot on. It was the wrong foot. He pulled it off, looked at both boots very seriously, and tried the other one. Rafael checked his watch and made himself sit on the stairs. Three minutes later both wellies were on. Liam stood up, splashed in the doorway puddle, and said, 'I did it all.'

qa.q: What colour were Liam's wellies?
qa.a: Liam's wellies were green.

qa.q: How did Liam feel when he said 'I did it all'?
qa.a: He felt proud and pleased, because he had done it all by himself.

qa.q: What was wise about Rafael sitting on the stairs?
qa.a: It gave Liam room to finish on his own, supporting his healthy wish to do things himself even though they were in a hurry.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel checking his watch?
qa.a: Rafael probably felt impatient and a bit stressed about the bus, but chose to wait.

grounding: A young child insists on pulling on his own boots though the bus is due, and his father makes room for it.

passage: After nap time at the preschool, the class was lining up for the garden. Vasudha sat by the cubbies with her sandals. 'Need help?' asked Farida Ma'am. Vasudha shook her head hard. 'Vasudha do it.' She pushed one foot in, pulled the strap, missed the sticky part, and tried again. The line started to wiggle. Farida Ma'am asked the others to count the flowers painted on the wall while they waited. Vasudha tried five times. On the sixth, the strap stuck. She held both feet up high. 'See!' Everyone clapped, and the line marched out.

qa.q: What did Farida Ma'am ask the others to do while they waited?
qa.a: She asked them to count the flowers painted on the wall.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha shake her head hard at the offer of help?
qa.a: She wanted to do it herself and felt determined, even though the strap kept missing.

qa.q: How did Farida Ma'am support Vasudha's wish?
qa.a: She respected the 'no', kept the other children busy counting flowers, and let Vasudha keep trying until she succeeded.

qa.q: What was the waiting like for the other children?
qa.a: They got a bit wiggly, but counting flowers kept them busy, and they clapped when she managed it.

grounding: A young child insists on fastening her own sandals while the class waits, and her teacher makes room for that wish.

passage:
Monday (a foggy winter morning): Ritu Didi held out Hansa's woollen socks and shoes. “I'll do it, we're late.” Hansa pulled her feet away. “Me! I do it!” It took ten minutes. The school van honked twice.
Wednesday: Hansa sat on the step, tongue out, pushing the strap through the buckle. Didi waited, arms folded, but didn't take over. Six minutes.
Saturday: Hansa put on both shoes by herself, stood up, and stamped her feet. “See? Myself!” Didi clapped. Hansa ran to the gate with her chin up high.

qa.q: How long did putting on the shoes take on Monday?
qa.a: It took ten minutes, and the school van honked twice.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when she stamped her feet on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased, showing off that she could do it herself.

qa.q: What did Ritu Didi try on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: She waited without taking over, giving Hansa the chance to practise doing it herself.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu Didi on Monday when the van honks?
qa.a: Ritu Didi likely feels impatient and stressed about being late, while Hansa just wants to do it herself.

grounding: The three winter mornings show a young child insisting on putting on her own shoes although they are late, and her strong wish to do it herself.

passage:
It was Onam morning and raining hard. The auto was waiting at the gate, and Sudha Amma still had the sadya leaves to carry.
“Lakshmi, sandals, quick. Let me.”
“No! I do it!” Lakshmi sat on the wet step and pushed her foot in. Wrong foot. She took it out and tried again. The auto driver tooted.
Amma breathed in and out. Then she held the umbrella over Lakshmi and waited.
Left sandal. Right sandal. One strap stuck. Lakshmi pulled it with both hands, face scrunched.
Click.
“Done!” She jumped up, splashing a puddle, and grabbed Amma's hand, grinning.

qa.q: What was Sudha Amma still carrying?
qa.a: She still had the sadya leaves to carry.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when the strap clicked?
qa.a: She felt proud and delighted, jumping up and grinning because she did it herself.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped, even though they were late?
qa.a: She held the umbrella over Lakshmi and waited, letting her finish on her own.

qa.q: What might the auto driver think as he waits in the rain?
qa.a: The auto driver might feel impatient, not knowing how much doing it herself matters to Lakshmi.

grounding: The passage shows a young child insisting on putting on her own sandals on a rainy festival morning even though they are late.

passage:
On Ganesh Chaturthi morning, drums were already booming down the lane. Santosh Chacha was ready, with the flowers, at the door.
“Darshan, we'll miss the aarti! Give me your foot.”
“No! Myself!” Darshan grabbed his new shoes and sat on the floor.
He pushed his toes in. The heel folded. He pulled it out. Tried again. His lip wobbled, but when Chacha reached down, Darshan turned his whole body away.
Chacha sat on the step and waited.
Finally, both shoes were on. The laces were loose, but on. Darshan stood up very straight and marched to the door. “Now we go.”

qa.q: What was booming down the lane?
qa.a: Drums were already booming down the lane.

qa.q: Why did Darshan turn his whole body away when Chacha reached down?
qa.a: He badly wanted to do it himself and felt frustrated but determined, even though it was hard.

qa.q: What could Santosh Chacha try on the next busy morning?
qa.a: He could start getting ready a little earlier so Darshan has time to put on his own shoes.

qa.q: How might Santosh Chacha feel sitting on the step waiting?
qa.a: Chacha might feel impatient about missing the aarti, but also a little proud of Darshan's determination.

grounding: The passage shows a young child insisting on putting on his own shoes on a festival morning even though they are running late.

passage:
"Kamal, we'll be late for the Diwali show!"
"I do it myself, Mumma!"
Kamal sat on the step with his new shoes. He pushed his foot in. It went in sideways.
"Let me help."
"No! Myself!"
Binita took a breath and crouched beside him. "Okay. You do it. I'll hold the other shoe."
He pulled. He wriggled. His tongue poked out. At last the foot slid in.
"I did it!"
"You did," said Binita, smiling, and picked up the second shoe for him to try.

qa.q: What did Kamal say when Binita offered to help?
qa.a: He said, "No! Myself!"

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when his foot finally slid in?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, shouting "I did it!"

qa.q: What did Binita do well even though they were late?
qa.a: She took a breath, let Kamal do it himself, and helped only by holding the other shoe.

qa.q: What might Binita have been feeling as they ran late?
qa.a: Binita was probably a little anxious about the time, but chose patience.

grounding: A small boy insists on putting on his own shoes though they are late for a Diwali show, a strong, healthy wish to do it himself.

passage:
Daycare note, monsoon week, by Thomas
Rain again. Time to go out to the covered play area. Yamini sat on the floor with her yellow gumboots. I offered help. She said, "No! Me do it!" and pulled the boot the wrong way round. Then the right way. Then her sock came off. The others were already outside. She didn't cry. She tried five times. When the boot finally went on, she stamped it and laughed.
What I did next: I started calling boot time ten minutes earlier so she can do it herself without rushing. 🙂

qa.q: What colour were Yamini's gumboots?
qa.a: They were yellow gumboots.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when the boot finally went on?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, stamping it and laughing.

qa.q: Why did Thomas start calling boot time ten minutes earlier?
qa.a: So Yamini could keep doing it herself without rushing, supporting her healthy wish to act on her own.

qa.q: What might it feel like for Yamini to be the last one inside?
qa.a: She might feel a little left behind, but her own success seemed to matter more to her.

grounding: A daycare note shows a small child insisting on putting on her own gumboots even while the others go out, a strong, healthy wish.

passage: On Pongal morning, the bullock cart was waiting at the gate for the temple fair. Preeti sat on the doorstep with her new silver-strapped chappals. "I'll do it!" Her older brother Hrithik reached down. "Let me, the cart is going." "No! Me!" She pushed the strap over her heel. It slipped off. She tried again. Amma called from the gate. Hrithik sighed and sat down next to her. He waited. The strap slipped a third time. On the fourth, it held. Preeti jumped up and ran to the cart, holding her skirt, beaming. "I did it all by myself!"

qa.q: What was waiting at the gate?
qa.a: The bullock cart was waiting at the gate.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when the strap finally held?
qa.a: Preeti felt proud and delighted, beaming as she ran to the cart.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped, even though the cart was waiting?
qa.a: He stopped trying to do it for her and sat down to wait, letting her finish by herself.

qa.q: How might Amma feel waiting at the gate?
qa.a: Amma was probably a little impatient, wanting to reach the fair.

grounding: On Pongal morning a small girl insists on fastening her own chappals while the cart waits, a strong, healthy wish to act herself.

passage:
The first snow had come to Leeds overnight, and nursery started in ten minutes. Kwame held out Sami's boots. "Quick, let me do them."
"No! Me do it!" Sami grabbed the boots and sat on the hall mat. He pushed his foot into one. Wrong boot. He pulled it out, frowned, tried the other. The strap wouldn't go through the loop.
Kwame looked at the clock, reached out, then pulled his hand back and waited, keys jingling.
The strap went through. Sami stood, stamped both feet and beamed. "I did it my own self!"
They were seven minutes late.

qa.q: What happened the first time Sami pushed his foot in?
qa.a: He pushed his foot into one boot, but it was the wrong boot.

qa.q: How did Sami feel when the strap went through?
qa.a: Sami was proud and delighted; he beamed, stamped his feet and said, "I did it my own self!" 😊

qa.q: What did Kwame do well, even though they were late?
qa.a: Kwame held back from taking over and waited, so Sami could finish by himself; next time they might simply start a little earlier.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Kwame?
qa.a: It was probably stressful for Kwame, watching the clock with the keys in hand, but he chose Sami's chance to do it himself over being on time.

grounding: A small child insists on putting on his own boots although they are late, showing a strong, healthy wish to act by his own will.
